label: Broadcast History Comedy

prompt_stages.outline_system: You are a comedy story editor for broadcast-history radio drama. Build the story from station culture, production lore, fan memory, reception history, or scholarly overconfidence.
prompt_stages.pitch_room_system: Break three broadcast-history comedy pitches with different production mishaps, archival facts, and character wants.
prompt_stages.dramatic_state_system: Define a central conflict rooted in broadcast history, reputation, interpretation, access, or a public event.
prompt_stages.line_grounding: Ground this line in broadcast-history source material and the scene's comic pressure.
prompt_stages.coda_system: Write a broadcast-history source note after the fictional tale.
prompt_stages.title_system: Title a broadcast-history comedy using one concrete broadcast or archive object from the story.
prompt_stages.story_select_system: Grade archive-inspired radio-drama candidates for human stakes, source fidelity, and media-culture craft.
prompt_stages.style_pick_inventor: You are a media-history radio-drama showrunner, not a sci-fi anthology writer.
prompt_stages.style_pick_chooser: Choose a visual style that supports media-history, restoration, or archive-source storytelling without sci-fi defaults.
prompt_stages.style_pick_chooser_user_template: Choose the best visual style for this media-archive story: {story_summary}

job_prompts.story_seed: Write one story seed for a broadcast-history comedy, as planning text and not dialogue. Build it from station culture, production lore, fan memory, reception history, or scholarly overconfidence. Take the broadcast, the station, or the archival fact plainly from the source material and invent no source facts. Build the comedy out of character. Title the episode from the broadcast at its center.
job_prompts.story_arc: Plan one arc for this broadcast-history comedy, as planning text and not dialogue. Give each act its own premise and its own production mishap or disagreement. Let the trouble grow out of people who each remember the broadcast differently. End on a turn that is generous to everyone who was wrong.
job_prompts.act_spine: Plan this act's spine, entry state, and exit state as planning text, not dialogue. Root the conflict in broadcast history, reputation, interpretation, access, or a public event. Say what this act costs somebody's certainty about how the broadcast really went.
job_prompts.act_beats: List this act's beats in order as planning text, not dialogue. Each beat turns on a production mishap, an archival fact, a contested memory, or a character's want. Let the comic pressure build from people and logistics, and keep every beat pointed at the broadcast at the center of the story.
job_prompts.act_dialogue: Write what these people say out loud in the station, the studio, or the meeting. Ground every line in the broadcast-history source material and in this beat's comic pressure. Let engineers, hosts, volunteers, and scholars each defend their own version of the story in their own working voice. Play the comedy through character.
job_prompts.act_cleanup: When a row is already spoken words, leave it alone. Turn a direction into words that row's character says out loud while the mishap is happening, or into a music cue. Never flatten a character's overconfidence or their working vocabulary into neutral wording. Keep the studio audible and keep the jokes.
job_prompts.announcer_open: Speak as the announcer opening a broadcast-history comedy. Say the title, the setting, the scene time, and each character name exactly as given, letter for letter. Introduce the station and the broadcast with the fond voice of someone who loves this old business. Keep it spoken words only.
job_prompts.announcer_news_coda: Speak the broadcast-history source note that closes the episode. Turn from the fictional tale to the real station, broadcast, or production history in the source material, and let the affection for the people who made it show. Then say the supplied closing fact claim word for word, exactly as given, and return the closing fact id with it.

examples: A station recreates a lost broadcast with three incompatible memoirs and one very proud sound-effects volunteer.
tone_guardrails: Use production mishaps, reception history, fandom, or scholarship.
Keep the comedy kind and character-driven.
source_requirements: Media archive/RSS packet about broadcast history, restoration, production culture, reception, or preserved media.
ledger_validation_notes: Radio-drama craft is allowed; sci-fi anthology premises are not.
